props.title: Night of the Zombies
props.initialSlug: Soldiers battle Nazi zombies in a remote mountain base

sections.content: Night of the Zombies, also known as "Hell of the Living Dead" or "Virus," represents the height of Italian zombie exploitation cinema that followed in the wake of George Romero's Dawn of the Dead (1978). Director Bruno Mattei, working under the pseudonym Vincent Dawn, created a bizarre mashup of stock footage, borrowed music from Goblin, and deliberately imitated scenes from both Romero's films and Zombie Flesh Eaters (1979). The film's wild combination of eco-horror themes, anti-colonial subtext, and gratuitous gore exemplifies the anything-goes approach of early 1980s Italian horror.

sections.content: The Italian zombie wave of 1979-1983 produced dozens of imitators trying to capture the success of Romero and Fulci. Burial Ground (1981) and Zombi 3 (1988) continued the tradition of mixing social commentary with excessive violence. What makes Night of the Zombies particularly noteworthy is its ambitious but clumsy attempt to incorporate real documentary footage of Papua New Guinea tribes into its narrative about a chemical leak causing a zombie outbreak.

The film's use of stolen music from Dawn of the Dead (1978) - specifically Goblin's iconic progressive rock score - sparked controversy but became common practice in Italian exploitation cinema. Similar music theft appeared in Contamination (1980) and Zombie Creeping Flesh (1982), showing how these low-budget productions often borrowed liberally from more successful films. sections.content: While most Italian zombie films focused purely on gore, Night of the Zombies attempted to incorporate environmental themes similar to Cannibal Holocaust (1980) and The Beyond (1981). The plot about a chemical facility accident causing zombification predates similar themes in Return of the Living Dead (1985) and shows early attempts to merge eco-horror with zombie mythology.
